description.value: Followers of Azal who separated from Baháʼuʼlláh following his public declaration in Edirne, remaining technically Bábís and retaining a stance of militancy and political activism. Following accusations of sedition lodged by the Azalís against Baháʼuʼlláh, the Ottoman government investigated and ultimately banished Baháʼuʼlláh to Acre and Azal to Cyprus.

The definitive schism between the Azalís and Baháʼís occurred in Adrianople (Edirne) between 1866 and 1868. While most Bábís accepted Baháʼuʼlláh's claim to be 'Him whom God shall make manifest' and became Baháʼís, the minority remaining loyal to Azal and the Bayán were referred to as Azalís or Azalí Bábís.

This persistent persecution acted as a major catalyst driving Baháʼís to flee Iran and establish communities in Russian-administered territories such as Transcaspia and the Caucasus.

description.value: Valentin Alekseevich Zhukovskii was a Russian Orientalist specializing in Persian language and dialects, literature, folklore, history, and ethnography. He served as a professor at St Petersburg University (1886–1918), dean of the Faculty of Oriental Languages (1902–1911), and director of the Educational Department of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (1905–1917), and was a corresponding member of the Russian Academy of Sciences from 1899.

A student and close friend of Baron Viktor Rozen, he also collected documents and information regarding Bábís and Baháʼís during his travels in Iran and Transcaspia.

description.value: Nikolai Karlovich Girs (Nicholas de Giers) was a Russian diplomat of Scandinavian Protestant ancestry who worked in the Asian Department of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs from 1838 and was appointed first secretary in Istanbul in 1850. He served as minister in Ṭihrán from 1863, director of the Asian Department and deputy minister of foreign affairs from 1875, and minister of foreign affairs from 1882.

description.value: Matvei Avel’evich Gamazov was a Russian diplomat, translator, teacher of Turkish in the Educational Department of Oriental Languages of the Asian Department of the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and head of the department from 1872 to 1893. He was Aleksandr Tumanskii’s teacher and interested him in the study of Bábism.

description.value: In Russian accounts in Transcaspia, local Christians viewed the Bábís with high sympathy, placing them, relative to morality, immensely higher than Persians who did not adhere to their teaching. The religion's texts were characterized as having a moral-religious content and forming a high moral-social system that appeals to lofty ideals in daily life.

description.value: French diplomat and author who held diplomatic posts in Europe from 1849 to 1854 before serving in Ṭihrán as first secretary of the French legation (1855), chargé d'affaires (1856–1858), and minister in Iran (1862–1863). His account of the Bábí movement in Les religions et les philosophies dans l'Asie centrale was widely influential.

description.value: Nikolai Vladimirovich Khanykov (1822–1878) was a Russian diplomat and Orientalist who served in the diplomatic department in the Caucasus and as head of the consulate-general in Tabríz. A corresponding member of the St Petersburg Academy of Sciences, he authored numerous scientific publications in history, geography, and ethnology, and collected Bábí manuscripts.

description.value: Vasilii Vladimirovich Bartol’d was a Russian Orientalist who specialized in the history of the Middle East, making his primary contribution in the medieval history of Central Asia and Iran. Born in St Petersburg to a Russianized German family, he studied under Viktor Rozen at St Petersburg University, where he taught from 1896 until the end of his life. Over his career, he published 670 works, including 247 articles in the Encyclopedia of Islam.

In 1924, he purchased the 'Hudud al-'Alam' ('Tumanskii's Manuscript') from Tumanskii's widow and transferred it to the Asiatic Museum / Institute of Oriental Studies, later publishing a facsimile edition in 1930.

description.value: Russian diplomat and author who served in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and in the Russian religious mission in China and Korea. He collected ethnographic information about Korea that formed the basis of his posthumously published book, Ocherki Korei (Sketches of Korea), and was heading the Russian diplomatic mission in Tehran as chargé d’affaires when he died at his post.

In its efforts to strengthen its influence in Iran, it secured economic monopolies and supported politicians such as Ẓill al-Sulṭán, while refraining from intervening on behalf of the persecuted Bábís so as not to alienate the Persian clergy and population.

description.value: Mírzá Taqí Khán, Amír Kabír, served as prime minister of Iran under Náṣir al-Dín Sháh Qájár, influencing the monarch to begin introducing reforms. In 1850, he ordered the transfer and execution of the Báb, assigning the execution to his brother Mírzá Ḥasan Khán Vazír-i Niẓám.

description.value: In 1850, the Báb was executed by firing squad in Tabríz. One of his chief adherents, Muḥammad-ʻAlí Zunúzí, was subjected to the same fate alongside him.

description.value: The death of Baháʼuʼlláh occurred on the morning of 16 May 1892 (Old Style) in his mansion (qaṣr) at Bahjí near ʻAkká. He had lived in the vicinity of the city for the remainder of his life following his banishment to Acre in 1868.

description.value: A commercial concession granted in 1890 by Náṣir al-Dín Sháh to a British company, secured with the assistance of Mírzá ‘Alí-Aṣghar Khán. It sparked intense opposition and protests from the clergy and the Iranian public, forcing the Sháh to cancel and revoke the concession in 1892.

The widespread opposition is often referred to as the Tobacco Protest or Tobacco Movement (1891–1892), famously catalyzed by a fatwá issued by Grand Ayatollah Mírzá Ḥasan Shírází.

description.value: The assassination in 1896 of Náṣir al-Dín Sháh Qájár, the ruler of Iran, followed his growing unpopularity late in his reign. The murder provoked heightened anti-Baháʼí sentiment as well as rumors and press reports alleging that Bábís or Baháʼís were involved in the plot.
description.source: Shahvar et al., The Baha'is of Iran, Transcaspia and the Caucasus, vol. 1, p. 202 (biographical note); vol. 2, p. 179 (biographical note); vol. 1, p. 26; vol. 2, p. 85–6; vol. 2, p. 90

description.value: In 1848, the Báb was brought to Tabríz and interrogated before the Valíʻahd (crown prince) and members of the Shiʻi clergy, where he declared himself to be the long-awaited Imám. He was subsequently declared an apostate by the ʻulamá.

In Bahá'í and Qajar historiography, the examination in Tabríz before Crown Prince Náṣiri'd-Dín Mírzá is generally dated to July 1848 (unverified).

description.value: In 1852, several Bábís made an unsuccessful assassination attempt on the life of Náṣir al-Dín Sháh in revenge for the execution of the Báb. The sháh survived and retaliated with severe persecutions, resulting in the arrest, torture, and execution of many Bábís and suspected conspirators, as well as the imprisonment and eventual exile of Baháʼuʼlláh.

description.value: Following persecution and pressure on the Baháʼí community in Iran, Baháʼuʼlláh encouraged Baháʼís to emigrate to Ashgabat after Russia established control over the region. Russian authority offered security, work, and land, with the first Baháʼí refugees arriving in Ashgabat in 1884 after facing persecution in Iṣfahán, Yazd, and Sabzivár.

description.value: The execution of seven Baháʼís on 19 May 1891 by order of the governor of Yazd, Jalál al-Dawlih, at the instigation of the local mujtahid Shaykh Ḥasan Sabzivárí. The persons behind the executions are thought to have been Ẓill al-Sulṭán and his son Jalál al-Dawlih.

preferred_label.value: Russian recognition of the Baháʼí religion

description.value: Following a public murder intended to trigger a pogrom against the Baháʼís in Russian-administered Transcaspia, Russian authorities under General Aleksandr Vissarionovich Komarov rejected arguments that the incident was merely an internal Iranian religious dispute. In November 1890, a special military tribunal sent from St Petersburg tried the suspects, sentencing the two murderers to death and other conspirators to exile in Siberia, imprisonment, and deportation.

The provided excerpt (vol. 1, pp. 17–18) mentions Russian diplomatic relations, Dolgorukov, Tsar Alexander II, and Iran, but does not mention or describe the Russian conquest of Central Asia; therefore, description and dates cannot be established from the source text. Náṣir al-Dín Sháh viewed the verdict as Russian recognition of the Baháʼís and joined with Rukn al-Dawlih and the Shiʻi clerical establishment of Mashhad to petition Russian authorities and the tsar to remit or overturn the sentences.

description.value: A war fought between 1853 and 1856 in which Russia suffered territorial losses in the Balkans and along the northern shore of the Black Sea, damaging Russian military prestige.

The fortunes of the Baháʼís in Iran briefly improved with the wartime occupation of Iran by Russian and British forces, though this relief was short-lived and followed by brutal repression.

In January 1867, Shaykh Aḥmad and two other leaders were executed, while the Persian authorities left the remaining detainees to the judgment of the ʻulamáʼ with the intention of pardoning those who recanted.

After their teaching spread among Persians and Turks, the Adrianople authorities imprisoned the Persian emigrants on instructions from the Porte and sold their property, and they were sent into exile to ʻAkká, as reported from Adrianople in August 1868.

description.value: A decision of the Anti-religious Commission of the Central Committee of the All-Union Communist Party (Bolsheviks), taken at its meeting in Moscow on 14 December 1928 (Protocol No. 105), to liquidate the "Behaist" (Baháʼí) organization within the borders of the USSR in view of its alleged anti-Soviet and spying character, and to report on the Behaists' activity in Bezbozhnik and Izvestiia.

description.value: The successive banishments of Baháʼuʼlláh and his family and companions. After the attempt on the life of Náṣiri'd-Dín Sháh in 1852 he was imprisoned in the Síyáh-Chál; found innocent, he was released but sent into exile. He arrived in Baghdad on 8 April 1853, and from 1854 spent two years alone in the mountains of Kurdistan before returning. In 1863 he was exiled further to Istanbul, after a few months sent on to Adrianople (Edirne), and in 1868 banished to ʻAkká, where he lived for the rest of his life.

A different account is given by Nabíl-i Aʻẓam in The Dawn-Breakers.

It commemorates Baháʼuʼlláh's stay in the Najíbíyyih or Riḍván Garden in Baghdad in 1863, before his departure from the city, during which he first announced his prophetic station to the companions present.

preferred_label.value: Baháʼuʼlláh's declaration in the Garden of Riḍván

description.value: Baháʼuʼlláh's announcement of his prophetic station to the companions present, that he was 'he whom God shall make manifest', during his twelve-day stay in the Najíbíyyih or Riḍván Garden in Baghdad from 21 April to 2 May 1863, before his departure from the city. It is commemorated each year by the Festival of Riḍván.
description.source: Shahvar et al., The Baha'is of Iran, Transcaspia and the Caucasus, vol. 1, p. 209 (glossary); vol. 2, p. 208 (editors' note 23); vol. 2, p. 218 (editors' note 98)

draft_notes: Dates from the editors' glossary (v1 p. 209, which misprints the year as 1963) and notes 23 and 98 (v2 pp. 208, 218; note 98 corrects a document that put it in 1864). The index heading 'Ridwan' also refers to the festival (e.g. v1 p. 132).

preferred_label.value: E. G. Browne's visit to Baháʼuʼlláh

variant_labels.value: Meeting of Baháʼuʼlláh and E. G. Browne

description.value: The visit of the Cambridge orientalist Edward Granville Browne to Baháʼuʼlláh at his residence near ʻAkká in 1890, during which Browne was received by Baháʼuʼlláh and recorded his words on the unity of nations and religions ('That all nations should become one in faith and all men as brothers').
description.source: Shahvar et al., The Baha'is of Iran, Transcaspia and the Caucasus, vol. 2, p. 120; vol. 2, p. 149; vol. 2, pp. 153–154

draft_notes: Year 1890 confirmed by the reviewer. The document on v2 p. 120 says Browne met Baháʼuʼlláh 'twice'; Browne's own account records four interviews, at the mansion of Bahjí, in April 1890 (usually 15–20 April): unverified here, so not in the description or dates.

preferred_label.value: Tablet of Baháʼuʼlláh predicting cholera and plague (unidentified)

title: Unidentified tablet of Baháʼuʼlláh predicting cholera and plague

description.value: A short tablet sent by Baháʼuʼlláh from ʻAkká to his followers in Persia, predicting that cholera and plague (vabá va al-ṭáʻún) would befall Persia, accompanied by a prayer beginning 'Huwa al-Mushfiq al-Karím' whose reading would protect the faithful from these diseases. A copy was obtained by a Russian consular official in Astrabad, who described it in a letter to Viktor Rozen.
description.source: Shahvar et al., The Baha'is of Iran, Transcaspia and the Caucasus, vol. 1, p. 175

draft_notes: Not identified in bahai-data's works. The incipit of the prayer (Huwa al-Mushfiq al-Karím) may identify it; once found, this record should redirect to that work. 'Letter to Viktor Rozen' is inferred from the letters' context (unverified).

description.value: An assassination attempt in Edirne in which Mírzá Yaḥyá (Azal) attempted to kill his half-brother Baháʼuʼlláh by poisoning.
description.source: Shahvar et al., The Baha'is of Iran, Transcaspia and the Caucasus, vol. 2, p. 168; vol. 2, p. 215n

draft_notes: Year 1865 confirmed by the reviewer (the book's passages don't give it). The sources place this event in Edirne (between Baháʼuʼlláh's arrival in late 1863 and his banishment to Acre in 1868) but do not give an exact date. From general knowledge (unverified), the poisoning occurred around 1865 or 1866 and left Baháʼuʼlláh with a persistent tremor.
